01 Founding TSMC and the dedicated foundry model▶

01 Founding TSMC and the dedicated foundry model

B LIFE-H01-001 | H01-J | Type B — retrospective interpretive comparison

乾：元亨。利貞。

Great success and openness; perseverance in what is right brings benefit.

Established in 1987, TSMC chose to manufacture chips designed by other companies. This division of labor required considerable investment in production technology, delivery reliability, confidentiality, and customer trust. Incorporation established a direction, not an accomplished business: orders, manufacturing trials, and consistent deliveries had to follow.

The background to this case was the business model. The surviving account must be read from that starting point rather than from the outcome alone. It describes a specific historical setting, with decisions and practical obligations that arose in that setting. The source does not supply a complete contemporaneous record of every participant’s actions, and it should not be made to do so.

The next part of the recorded sequence concerns formation of the company. This is the central action described in the Traditional Chinese source. The order of events matters: the question existed before the response, and the eventual outcome was not yet known when the action was taken. The case can be followed through the institutions, recorded decisions and practical steps mentioned in the source, without adding conversations or private thoughts.

The subsequent part concerns production and delivery. This belongs after the preceding actions, not before them. The later record may describe what followed or how a historian presented those consequences; it does not give a complete day-by-day account. Where details are absent, such as individual discussions, exact amounts, or intermediate events, the account makes no claim that those details are known.

Taken together, the documented sequence runs from the business model, through formation of the company, and finally to production and delivery. These phases explain what occasioned the event, what action is reported, and what can be said about its aftermath. The narrative remains distinct from the modern comparison with the Zhouyi: unless the case is explicitly classed as a documented use of the text, it does not claim that the historical participants used this hexagram to choose their course.

Before launching a business or changing careers, define what you can deliver, which capabilities are necessary, and how you will honor commitments over time. A clear promise needs repeatable execution. The historical sequence began with the business model, passed through formation of the company, and left the later question of production and delivery. That distinction matters for everyday choices: an attractive intention is not the same as an action that can be carried out, and a recorded result does not reveal every reason why it happened. For a workplace or personal decision, ask what information is actually available, whose interests are affected, and what responsibility remains after the first step. Write down the practical conditions that would let others check whether a promise has been met. Do not treat a classical image as a prediction or a substitute for evidence. This is a Type B retrospective analogy. The historical participants are not shown to have used this hexagram to make the decision. Question to carry forward: What capability would substantiate your professional promise?

02 Nan Kuai seeks support for a rebellion in an auspicious reading

A LIFE-H02-001 | H02-L5 | Type A — documented quotation / divination

六五：黃裳，元吉。

A yellow lower garment; supreme good fortune.

Nan Kuai contemplated rebelling against the Ji family and interpreted an apparently favorable divination as support. Zifu Huibo warned that the words about the yellow lower garment required loyalty and appropriate conduct, not merely a fortunate ending. Nan Kuai rebelled but lost local support and fled to Qi. The Zuozhuan records competing interpretations, not supernatural causation.

Keep rest and restraint after a milestone. The source manuscript links this decision theme to Early Han Recovery and Its Fiscal Limits. After the civil conflicts surrounding the beginning of the Han dynasty, agriculture and public revenues had to be restored over time. Cultivation, tax collection, and the management of grain and money were connected: the treasury could accumulate reserves only as a functioning productive base returned. Its history provides a concrete setting in which responsibilities, resources and consequences became visible.

Apply the idea to a real situation rather than to a slogan. After reaching a major goal, protect the time and resources needed for the next phase instead of spending the entire surplus. Separate what is known from what still needs confirmation. Agree on one responsible person and one review date. If the plan creates a burden for someone else, make that burden visible before proceeding.

In the Xiao Xiang translation: “Drinking until the head is wet shows failure to recognize moderation.” The text does not establish a cause-and-effect rule for present-day decisions. This is a later comparison, and the historical account should not be credited with words, intentions or outcomes absent from the sources.

The Records of the Grand Historian describes the Cao Bing family as having built a business from iron production. Smelting and dealing in iron could create income, but an established workshop did not by itself determine how household wealth would be retained or used. The family had to make choices about everyday spending and the deployment of resources beyond its original line of work.

The account describes a combination of ironworking, frugal household habits, lending, and commerce across places. Income from production was not treated as identical to money available for unlimited consumption. The family kept expenditure under restraint while engaging in other transactions. Lending moved resources to borrowers and created the possibility of repayment or default. Trade across localities required merchandise to circulate between markets, where transport and changes in demand mattered.

These activities were not one instantaneous act of investment. They formed a sequence in which productive work provided a foundation, household management affected the amount retained, and lending or trade opened additional channels for circulating wealth. The historical text summarizes the family’s economic conduct rather than presenting modern accounts with individual loan rates, trading dates, costs, or yearly returns. Rental terms had to be reflected in actual leases and local administration. Changes in the rental share affected the income received by landlords and the portion retained by the people working the land.

After the rule changed, both sides still had ongoing obligations. Farmers had to continue cultivating and landlords retained property interests that were not wholly resolved by lower rent. Zhao therefore appointed Lin Xiangru to travel to the Qin court with the jade and conduct the exchange.

After arriving, Lin Xiangru presented the object and observed that Qin had not immediately provided the promised cities. According to the Records of the Grand Historian, he obtained the jade back by offering to point out a flaw in it. He then challenged the manner in which the exchange was being handled and sought more formal conditions for the transfer. The surviving biography recounts an extended confrontation, including speeches. Because these speeches come through a later historian, their exact wording should not be treated as a verbatim transcript.

As discussions continued, Lin Xiangru arranged for the jade to be returned to Zhao. He remained at the Qin court to face the consequences. This separated the immediate task of safeguarding the object from the unresolved diplomatic dispute. The proposed exchange of cities for the jade was not completed. Qin did not obtain the object under the original terms, and Zhao did not receive the cities.

The episode can be followed from Qin's proposal, through Zhao's appointment of an envoy and the negotiations at court, to the return of the jade. It is a narrative preserved in the Shiji biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru, not a contemporary transcript of every meeting. The story ends not with an instant national transformation but with an identifiable village agreement entering a longer history of changes in agricultural organization. Original Chinese title: 1930年代白銀波動衝擊資金安排 | Period: 1933—1935年｜近現代｜本稿對照1次

Source caveat: 銀價、金融與景氣之間因果複雜；本例不把所有困難歸因於單一外國措施。

Historical event | Short narrative

In China during the early 1930s, silver remained closely connected to currency, banking, and settlement of payments. Banks and businesses depended on the availability of the metal within the domestic financial system. Changes in international silver markets and foreign policy altered demand for silver outside China, creating pressure for silver to flow out of the country.

From about 1933 to 1935, the movement of silver became a financial concern. The outflow placed pressure on bank liquidity and on businesses that depended upon credit and reliable settlement. Institutions including the Bank of China attempted to coordinate responses. Yet the difficulty arose from the interaction between world-market prices and China's domestic currency arrangements. A single bank, merchant, or local office could not remove the international incentives underlying the movement of the metal.

The issue did not end with an isolated banking decision. Subsequent monetary reform changed the relationship between silver and the new legal-tender system, forming a later institutional response to the crisis. Banking histories preserve the sequence of financial pressure, coordination, and policy change, but do not identify an identical shortage in every city or provide complete bank-by-bank accounts. Precise silver prices, quantities shipped, and individual losses would need separate statistical verification. The documented story therefore runs from an external market shift, through domestic monetary stress and attempts at coordination, to a broader reform of the currency framework. It should not be reduced to one day's price movement.

The available material identifies major actions and their sequence, not every participant's individual choices. Any more precise figures, private conversations, motives, or household-level outcomes would require evidence beyond the cited account. The story is accordingly confined to the measures and consequences actually described in the source, without presenting a later historical analogy as something the historical actors themselves said or believed. In this account, the initial problem, the recorded intervention, and the subsequent responsibility are distinguishable phases. No unrecorded conversation or psychological explanation is needed to establish that chronology.

In 635 BCE, disorder within the Zhou royal house forced King Xiang of Zhou away from his capital. The royal court's position created a question for neighboring rulers: whether to become involved in restoring the king, and what resources and political commitments an intervention would require. Duke Wen of Jin had already established a position among the regional lords. His adviser Hu Yan urged assistance to the Zhou king, presenting the matter as both a response to the royal crisis and an opportunity for Jin to strengthen its standing.

The Zuo Zhuan records that Duke Wen consulted divination and received the hexagram Da You changing to Kui. The transmitted interpretation included wording associated with the Son of Heaven. This consultation belongs to the recorded sequence, but it was not the only step. Jin still had to decide on action, organize military support and carry out the intervention. The surviving narrative describes political advice, divination and military action together; it does not reduce the operation to a prediction automatically producing its result.

Jin subsequently sent forces to help King Xiang return to the royal capital. Following the restoration, Jin received rewards. These developments changed Jin's relationship to the Zhou court and formed part of the broader political settlement. The reward was an aftermath of the intervention, not evidence that divination guaranteed success or that all possible costs had been removed.

The account is preserved in the Zuo Zhuan for the twenty-fifth year of Duke Xi of Lu, with a parallel tradition in the Xin Xu. The transmitted wordings differ in some places, including forms commonly rendered heng and xiang. The source manuscript treats this as an example of historical consultation of the Zhouyi, but it expressly does not claim that the actor quoted the Xiao Xiang line used in this edition. The modern analogy is therefore classified B for this line.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange was established in 1990 and formally opened for business on 19 December that year. Its creation provided an institutional setting for centralized securities trading. This marked a specific organizational change, not the immediate completion of every rule required for a mature market. Participants could come together around a trading venue, while the exchange and relevant authorities still needed to address the procedures used in listing, transactions, disclosure and supervision. The opening date is documented in the exchange's institutional history. That history does not provide a complete record of every trade executed by every investor.

After the exchange began operating, the work of organizing a securities market continued. Listed companies and market participants had to follow evolving requirements, while investors remained exposed to changes in security prices and the circumstances of individual companies. A common trading venue could make some procedures more consistent, but it did not remove the risk of losses. Nor does the existence of an exchange prove that every security was fairly valued or that every investor received the same result.

The sequence is therefore a demand for a more organized trading system, the establishment and opening of the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 1990, and the subsequent operation and development of market rules and oversight. These are the stages supported by the manuscript's reference to the exchange's official history. No unrecorded trading conversations, personal motives or precise investment returns are needed to tell the story. The institution's founding was an identifiable event; the effectiveness of its continuing operations is a separate subject for historical examination.

Hong Kong authorities intervened in the stock market in 1998 during financial-market turmoil. That intervention left the public sector with shareholdings. After the immediate operation, the authorities faced the question of how those holdings should be handled. The initial situation did not resolve itself through a title, proclamation, or single favorable moment. The people and institutions involved had to operate within the resources and responsibilities already present. What happened next therefore depended on practical steps, including how the proposed arrangement would be carried out in the setting described by the source.

In 1999, the Tracker Fund of Hong Kong was launched as part of a disposal arrangement. The fund offered a mechanism through which shares could return to investors under organized procedures. Managing the aftermath of intervention was a distinct task from the intervention itself. Implementation was a separate part of the sequence. The action described in the record had to reach the people, organizations, or transactions concerned. Its consequences could only emerge through what was actually done, not through the wording of the plan alone. The account does not provide an individual scene for every participant, so no such scenes are added here.

The launch did not erase the public risks of the earlier action. Hong Kong Monetary Authority records describe the fund and the disposal context. The chronology runs from market pressure, to public intervention, to the subsequent mechanism for handling the acquired shares. The later situation should not be treated as proof that every participant benefited equally. The surviving record identifies the broad result, while leaving some local or individual consequences outside its scope. The event can therefore be followed from the original conditions, through the recorded action, to what came afterward without filling those gaps with imagined detail. The available material gives the reader an identifiable beginning, an intervening course of action, and a subsequent condition. Those stages should be kept distinct: the need that prompted action is not itself an outcome, and a later outcome does not establish every detail of how participants experienced the change. The account is limited to the circumstances, actions, and consequences recorded for this event.

Original Chinese title: 四年經建計畫分期推進轉型 | Period: 1953年起｜近現代｜本稿對照1次

Source location: 1953年經濟建設四年計畫段

Source caveat: 漸進不保證沒有代價；農工之間資源轉移的負擔仍需另行研究。

Historical event | Short narrative

In the early 1950s, Taiwan faced the task of rebuilding productive capacity while finance, industrial materials, and equipment remained constrained. Agriculture supplied food and some raw materials; emerging industries required inputs, capital, and markets. Expanding each sector without arranging their respective roles would not automatically resolve these shortages. Public economic planning therefore had to address the order in which investments and supporting production could take place.

Beginning in 1953, Taiwan implemented its first Four-Year Economic Development Plan. The plan linked agricultural development with selected light industries and promoted some forms of import-substituting production. Its approach was not to make all industries self-sufficient immediately. Agriculture and industry were treated as sectors whose outputs and demands could support each other if resources were allocated in a practicable sequence. Plans were established across years rather than executed as a single purchase or construction project.

As the planning period unfolded, public investment had to be allocated and producers had to adjust within the available conditions. Farms and industrial enterprises did not change their operations at exactly the same time. The supplied historical account identifies the launch and broad priorities of the plan but does not provide a comprehensive annual reconciliation of every proposed target, expenditure, and achieved result. It therefore does not support a claim that the whole economic transition had been accomplished in 1953.

The sequence runs from limited postwar resources, through an integrated multi-year framework, to the gradual implementation and evaluation of the relationship between agricultural supply and industrial development. A four-year horizon established an organizational timetable, not an automatic guarantee of success. Source trace: TEN, the section on the development plan beginning in 1953.

The surviving account places this episode in an economic setting where the sequence of decisions mattered to those carrying out ordinary transactions or productive work. Its first stage established the circumstances for action; its next stage introduced the documented arrangement; and its later stage involved continuing obligations or effects. The record allows these stages to be distinguished, but does not supply complete individual accounts from which uniform gains or losses could be calculated.

Original Chinese title: 卓氏遷蜀：在不利處境中保存可用的本領 | Period: 秦滅趙後至漢初｜古代｜本稿對照2次

Original source codes: SJ129

Source location: 卓氏段

Source caveat: 這是強制遷徙背景，不能美化成自願創業旅行；史籍成功例也不代表所有遷徙者。

Historical event | Short narrative

The Records of the Grand Historian describes the Zhuo family as iron producers in the former state of Zhao. After Qin conquered Zhao, the family was forcibly relocated. The move interrupted its previous connection to local resources, facilities and markets. Iron production depended on technical knowledge, but it also required ore, a place to work and people who would purchase or exchange the finished products. The surviving passage does not inventory the property lost or transported during the relocation.

The Zhuo family chose Linqiong in the Shu region as the place to resume its livelihood. The historical account connects that choice with the availability of iron resources and opportunities for trade. Experience in ironworking could be used again, but a new location still required the family to connect its knowledge to local materials and buyers. The move was not a planned expansion from an undisturbed business. It followed military conquest and an imposed transfer of population.

The record subsequently associates the family with renewed iron production and the accumulation of wealth. It preserves the broad transition from displacement to rebuilding, rather than a day-by-day account of mining, smelting, hiring, sales or transport. It is possible to identify the sequence of the family's earlier trade, forced movement and later business activity. It is not possible to calculate a rate of return or reconstruct every commercial decision from this brief account.

The family's later wealth was recorded by Sima Qian in a discussion of commerce and production. That is the documented aftermath, not proof that the initial loss of place was harmless. Other displaced households may have faced very different outcomes, and this passage does not provide evidence about them. The account is useful because it shows a particular skill being employed in a new economic setting after upheaval. The story should retain both sides of the record: coercive relocation came first, and the opportunity to rebuild came afterward.

Original Chinese title: 晉獻公嫁伯姬前的占問 | Period: 春秋 記於前645年｜古代｜本稿對照1次

Original source codes: Y54、P054

Source location: 《左傳》僖公十五年及左傳正義

Source caveat: A類 用易記載。前645年是記事及韓原之戰年份，不是婚姻起筮的確定年份；史傳占辭與通行經文並非逐字相同。 本冊引用的是《小象傳》；史料所引《周易》卦爻辭不能據此認定其曾引用《小象傳》。

Historical event | Short narrative

In the Spring and Autumn period, marriages between ruling families could become part of relations between neighboring states. The Zuo Zhuan, in its account under the fifteenth year of Duke Xi, looks back to a marriage arranged by Duke Xian of Jin. He intended to marry Bo Ji into the ruling family of Qin. Before the marriage, a divination using the Changes was performed, producing Gui Mei changing to Kui. The historian Su read the result as unfavorable. The account preserves the adverse interpretation but does not show that the marriage arrangement was cancelled.

The marriage proceeded. The relationship between Jin and Qin then continued through changes of rulers, negotiations, grain-related dealings, and disputes. These later events involved political choices and circumstances beyond the earlier marriage. The Zuo Zhuan places the remembered divination in a narrative about the conflict that culminated in the Battle of Han Yuan in 645 BCE. The later passage includes discussion of whether the warning had been heeded. It is evidence of how the chronicler connected a remembered divination with later affairs, not proof that the marriage itself caused every subsequent dispute.

The record does not give Bo Ji an independent account of her wishes or experience. Nor does it establish the exact year in which the original divination occurred: 645 BCE is the date of the battle and the annalistic passage that recounts it. The surviving wording also belongs to a transmitted historical account and should not be silently substituted for a modern edition of the canonical line text.

The episode therefore has a limited but traceable sequence: a proposed diplomatic marriage, consultation of the Changes, an unfavorable interpretation, the marriage going ahead, and later developments in Qin–Jin relations. The source documents an act of divination concerning the Changes. It does not establish that Duke Xian or the historian Su consulted the later Xiao Xiang line commentary. That distinction matters when the episode is linked retrospectively to a line in this collection.

After the civil conflicts surrounding the beginning of the Han dynasty, agriculture and public revenues had to be restored over time. Cultivation, tax collection, and the management of grain and money were connected: the treasury could accumulate reserves only as a functioning productive base returned. A government with more stored resources could meet administrative needs and some unexpected demands without immediately seeking new funds.

The Book of Han describes the accumulation of considerable state stores following years of recovery. Grain stocks and public money grew during the period associated with Emperors Wen and Jing and the early Han period that followed. Such stores represented resources built up across multiple seasons and fiscal decisions. They were not the result of a single deposit made on one day or a guarantee that future expenditure would remain small.

The historical account also records a later change as major state spending increased, including under Emperor Wu. Public resources that had accumulated previously were drawn upon as obligations expanded. Earlier abundance and later fiscal pressure therefore belong to different stages of the sequence. It would misrepresent the narrative to describe the treasury as simultaneously accumulating and exhausting the same reserves at the same moment.

The episode proceeds from postwar recovery to stronger public stores and then to new spending pressures that reduced fiscal room. The cited sections establish the broad historical movement, not a modern consolidated budget with annual balances for every office. The amount available at one time could not alone determine what later commitments would cost. Original Chinese title: 師史跨地經商須適應陌生環境 | Period: 漢代｜古代｜本稿對照1次

Original source codes: ESJ129

Source location: 師史段

Source caveat: 史籍沒有完整交易清單；不能把成功商人的片段故事當成跨境經營保證。

Historical event | Short narrative

The Records of the Grand Historian includes the merchant Shi Shi of Luoyang among accounts of people who accumulated wealth through commerce. The source describes a business that did not depend solely on one shop or a single local market. Goods had to be moved between places, and that movement required both transport and people capable of handling transactions. For a merchant operating beyond familiar streets, distance created opportunities to reach buyers, but it also separated the owner from the daily work of buying, carrying, and selling.

Shi Shi organized trading journeys and made use of experienced assistants. Carts, goods, and entrusted workers were parts of the same undertaking. People traveling with merchandise needed to understand the route and the markets they encountered. The merchant could not personally oversee every stage in every place. Delegating work therefore mattered as much as having goods available to trade. The source emphasizes this organization and the resulting commercial success, without providing a full schedule of journeys.

As the journeys proceeded, the arrangements had to work in more than one setting. Transport linked the places where merchandise was obtained and the places where it could be sold. Those who acted on the merchant's behalf needed sufficient knowledge to carry out transactions in his absence. The surviving account gives the broad pattern of this activity rather than individual invoices, exact sale prices, or a complete record of payments. It does not identify a particular storm, robbery, or negotiation that can be turned into a dramatic scene.

The recorded outcome is that Shi Shi appears in the historian's discussion of prosperous merchants. That placement indicates how the source regarded his commercial activity, but it cannot establish the results of every journey or the circumstances of every worker. The sequence that can be responsibly retold is the formation of a trading operation, the dispatch of goods and capable personnel across regions, and the subsequent reputation for commercial success. It is a story of documented organization and movement, not a guarantee that leaving one's home market produces wealth.

Original Chinese title: 鄒忌藉生活觀察提醒齊王納諫 | Period: 戰國｜古代｜本稿對照1次

Original source codes: P055、P056

Source location: 《戰國策》齊策一 鄒忌脩八尺有餘

Source caveat: 後設對照。《戰國策》帶有辯說文學性，不能把一年後無可進諫當成全國問題已清零，更沒有用巽卦的直接證據。

Historical event | Short narrative

During the Warring States period, the court of Qi faced the familiar problem of how a ruler could hear criticism from people whose positions depended on him. The Zhanguo ce introduces this problem through a domestic episode involving Zou Ji. He asked his wife, a concubine and a visiting guest to compare his appearance with that of Xu Gong, a man known for his looks. Each answer favored Zou Ji. Their responses sounded consistent, but the people giving them did not occupy the same relationship to him.

When Zou Ji later saw Xu Gong, he judged that the favorable comparisons had not been reliable. The narrative explains the answers by reference to affection, apprehension and the hope of obtaining something. Zou Ji then took the example to King Wei of Qi. The point of his presentation was not to settle a contest of appearances. He described how the people surrounding a ruler might likewise withhold unwelcome judgments because of their dependence on him. The king's position made that problem potentially larger than the one within a household.

The account says that King Wei accepted the advice and announced rewards for different forms of remonstrance. Criticism delivered directly, written submissions and remarks circulating in public were given places within the arrangement. The narrative subsequently describes the number of remonstrances changing over time and presents the court as better able to receive information. These developments form the story's aftermath, as told in the text.

The Zhanguo ce is a collection shaped by persuasive rhetoric, not a transcript of each exchange. The dialogue and the reported progression of remonstrances should be read with that literary character in mind. In particular, fewer recorded complaints cannot establish that every difficulty in Qi had disappeared. What the surviving account preserves is a sequence: favorable answers in a household, a comparison that exposed their limitations, a presentation to the king and an announced channel for criticism. It does not show that Zou Ji or King Wei consulted the later Xiao Xiang commentary.

Original Chinese title: 鹽鐵會議把不同主張放在同一桌 | Period: 前81年｜古代｜本稿對照1次

Original source codes: ESALT

Source location: 〈本議〉雙方問答

Source caveat: 會議論辯不代表權力平等，也不能保證討論必然導致雙方滿意的改革。

Historical event | Short narrative

In 81 BCE, during the reign of Emperor Zhao of the Western Han, the court convened discussions about economic policies associated with the preceding reign. Government monopolies in salt and iron and related arrangements for moving and selling goods had become matters of controversy. State officials defended the resources these policies supplied for frontier defense and public expenditure. Scholars and other critics raised the effects on farmers, merchants and ordinary households. The two sides did not begin with the same measure of what counted as a benefit.

The discussion brought these positions into a shared forum. One argument concerned the revenue needed to maintain military commitments and administration. Another concerned prices, local livelihoods and the burden of government participation in commerce. When speakers discussed profit or public welfare, they sometimes referred to different beneficiaries and different time horizons. Questions could therefore be answered by disputing the assumptions behind them rather than by accepting a common set of figures. The exchanges also reflected unequal positions: participants were invited to speak, but they did not possess equal authority to determine policy.

The work known as the Yantie lun, or Discourses on Salt and Iron, later preserved an organized account of the arguments. It presents speakers responding to each other over multiple topics and lets later readers follow the lines of disagreement. The text is a literary and editorial record of debate, not an unedited stenographic transcript. It cannot establish the exact wording, duration or reception of every contribution at the meeting. Nor can one infer that the debate ended with complete agreement or immediate repeal of every disputed measure.

The documented sequence begins with established policies and criticism of their consequences, moves to a court-sponsored exchange of competing arguments and continues in a written record that circulated afterward. The surviving work makes the competing claims visible, while leaving the precise influence of particular speeches on subsequent decisions a separate historical question. This episode is paired with the Xiao Xiang retrospectively; the sources do not connect the participants' reasoning to that commentary.

Original Chinese title: 法幣改革整合分散支付制度 | Period: 1935年｜近現代｜本稿對照1次

Original source codes: EFABI、ETWO2

Source location: 1935年11月4日報告所錄改革措施

Source caveat: 法幣後來也面臨嚴重通膨，不能把建立共同規則等同永久成功。

Historical event | Short narrative

By the early 1930s, China's monetary system was under pressure from movements in the international price and supply of silver. Banks, merchants and households relied on payment arrangements that had to work across different places and contracts. As silver left the country and financial conditions tightened, continuing with existing practices became increasingly difficult. A currency reform could be announced centrally, but the practical change would still have to pass through bank counters, commercial accounts and everyday transactions.

In November 1935, the government announced the fabi reform. Banknotes issued by designated banks were established as legal currency, while rules concerning silver holdings and monetary arrangements were revised. The measures sought to bring payments into a more unified system. People and institutions holding silver had to consider the new requirements, and commercial parties had to decide how to settle obligations using the recognized means of payment. A legal declaration did not by itself complete every conversion or resolve every question of acceptance.

The next stage unfolded wherever money changed hands. Banks needed to apply the new rules to deposits and payments. Businesses needed to use the recognized currency when settling accounts, while individuals encountered the changes through wages, purchases and savings. The reform's intended coordination depended on these repeated transactions. Official announcements and contemporary reporting establish the date and broad measures, but they do not provide a complete record of how every locality or household adjusted.

The new arrangements provided a different basis for payment during the years that followed. They did not make the currency permanently stable. War, fiscal pressure and subsequent inflation severely weakened fabi in later years, and China eventually experienced further monetary changes. The story therefore runs from mounting pressure on the silver-based system, through the announcement and implementation of new payment rules, to later difficulties that exposed the limits of reform. Its use beside the Xiao Xiang is an editorial comparison, not evidence that the reformers consulted that commentary.

Original Chinese title: 商鞅徙木後真的支付賞金 | Period: 前4世紀｜古代｜本稿對照1次

Original source codes: P058、P059

Source location: 《史記》商君列傳 徙木記載

Source caveat: 後設對照。徙木故事具有示範性敘事特色；履行一次賞金，不表示整套法律都正當或對人民有利，也沒有直接用易證據。

Historical event | Short narrative

In the fourth century BCE, the Qin state prepared to introduce legal reforms associated with Shang Yang under Duke Xiao. A new set of rules could be drafted at court, but it would have to be followed by people outside the court. The Shiji, in its biography of Lord Shang, places a public demonstration between the preparation of the laws and their promulgation. The episode concerns a wooden pole, a short journey between city gates and a promised reward.

According to the account, a pole three zhang long was placed near the southern gate of the capital's marketplace. An announcement offered ten jin to anyone who carried it to the northern gate. No one initially accepted the task. The offered reward was then raised to fifty jin. One person moved the pole, and the promised fifty jin was paid. The text presents the payment as a visible demonstration that the announced terms would be honored. Only after this episode does the narrative say that the new laws were promulgated.

The story does not end with the movement of the pole. The Shiji continues with resistance to the new regulations and with harsh enforcement, including punishment connected with violations by members of the ruling household. It also recounts later assessments of the reforms and their effects on Qin. These subsequent passages matter because the payment of one reward is not evidence that every later measure was accepted freely or operated without harm. The reform program had consequences far beyond the small public task.

The surviving account offers a clear sequence: laws prepared, an announced task initially left undone, a larger reward offered and paid, and the laws then issued. Its form is also strongly exemplary; it is a historian's narrative, not a complete survey of public opinion. The source does not preserve the private thoughts of the person who carried the pole, and none are supplied here. The story can document how the Shiji presents a promise kept, without treating that incident as proof of the justice of the entire legal system or as a historical use of the Xiao Xiang.

Original Chinese title: 張氏從賣漿經營成家業 | Period: 漢代，史記所載｜古代｜本稿對照1次

Source location: 其他富人段「賣漿」記述

Source caveat: 史料未交代確切年代、成本或方法，因此不能補寫成完整創業傳奇。

Historical event | Short narrative

The Shiji's chapter on those who accumulated wealth does not confine its attention to rulers, officials or owners of large trading networks. Among its brief notices is a reference to a Zhang family associated with selling jiang, a prepared drink. The entry places an ordinary commercial activity among the ways people could acquire property. It does not begin with a dated account of the family's founding, and it gives no detailed description of a shop, its customers or its suppliers.

Selling a drink involves repeated exchanges rather than a single official appointment. Someone must have goods to offer, purchasers must be willing to pay and the receipts must be handled from one sale to the next. Those are basic conditions of the type of business named in the source, not specific facts about the Zhang family's methods. The Shiji does not tell us the family's recipe, premises, opening hours or costs. It also does not identify a sequence of decisions by which an individual seller gradually expanded into a larger enterprise.

What the historian does record is the connection between the trade and an accumulated family fortune. The result appears within a broader survey of commercial wealth, alongside other activities and places. This placement matters: a business that supplied an everyday product was considered worth mentioning in a discussion of wealth. Yet the brief notice leaves most of the intervening years undocumented. The reader can identify the activity and the reported outcome, but cannot reconstruct the intermediate steps with the precision available for better-documented political events.

The sequence that can safely be stated is limited. A family was associated with the sale of a common drink; the historian later included that activity in an account of wealth. No reliable narrative of a dramatic first customer, a special invention or a particular business crisis survives in this passage. The short record is therefore presented here with its gaps visible rather than turned into an invented entrepreneurial success story. Its pairing with the Xiao Xiang is a later analogy, not evidence that the family knew or applied the commentary.

Original source codes: EHS24B

Source caveat: 管理風險是本文件的分析，不是在聲稱這一批常平倉已被史料證明發生特定舞弊。

Historical event | Short narrative

Grain prices in the frontier commanderies of the Western Han empire changed with harvests and the availability of supplies. Farmers could receive low prices when grain was abundant, while buyers faced higher costs in short periods. If public authorities waited for a shortage before seeking food, procurement and transport would take additional time when demand was already pressing.

Geng Shouchang proposed establishing ever-normal granaries, or changpingcang, in which grain could be purchased when prices were low and sold when prices were high. This arrangement was designed to link storage with market conditions. By buying, keeping, and later releasing grain, the administration could hold stock between seasons rather than attempt all procurement during a shortage. Farmers selling after a harvest and households buying during scarcity were affected at different points in the cycle.

Granaries required upkeep and decisions as well as grain. Stocks had to be protected from loss, and officials needed to decide when to purchase or release them. The Book of Han describes the proposal and its operating principle, but does not establish that every granary in every year adjusted prices accurately or benefited all participants in the same degree. The sequence is a recognized problem with fluctuating prices, a proposal to acquire and store reserves, and later sales in response to demand. Storage converted an immediate purchase into the possibility of a future supply; the usefulness of that reserve still depended on maintenance and timing.

The available material identifies major actions and their sequence, not every participant's individual choices. Any more precise figures, private conversations, motives, or household-level outcomes would require evidence beyond the cited account. The story is accordingly confined to the measures and consequences actually described in the source, without presenting a later historical analogy as something the historical actors themselves said or believed. In this account, the initial problem, the recorded intervention, and the subsequent responsibility are distinguishable phases. No unrecorded conversation or psychological explanation is needed to establish that chronology.

English words: 336 | Canonical English version from batch 08

Original Chinese title: 金融重建基金階段處理完仍有未來風險 | Period: 2001—2011年｜近現代｜本稿對照1次

Original source codes: ERTC2、ERTC3

Source location: 基金期間、56家機構及處理原則

Source caveat: 後續風險提醒是編輯分析；本例沒有宣稱當前任何特定金融機構正處於危機。

Historical event | Short narrative

At the beginning of the twenty-first century, Taiwan faced the task of resolving problems at financial institutions whose condition threatened the continuity of banking services. A troubled institution could affect depositors, employees and the communities relying on its branches. Dealing with it required decisions about assets, liabilities and the transfer or termination of operations. In 2001, a financial restructuring fund was established to provide a legal mechanism for addressing such cases.

The fund operated through a defined period that extended to the end of 2011. Cases were not identical. Some institutions needed arrangements for another institution to assume business, while others required different forms of disposition. Depositors needed information about access to their funds, and the public needed an account of the use of the mechanism. Official material records that 56 troubled institutions were handled during the fund's period. That figure is an aggregate; it is not a complete history of the decision, cost and outcome for each institution.

The work continued beyond the initial identification of a problem. Legal procedures had to be followed, receiving institutions or other parties had to be identified where applicable, and the relevant records had to be preserved. The close of the authorized period supplied a point at which the program's scope and reported results could be reviewed. It did not mean that every future financial difficulty had been prevented, or that all issues affecting individual institutions ended on the same day.

The documented sequence begins with the creation of a public resolution mechanism, continues through the handling of individual troubled institutions and reaches a formal endpoint for the fund's designated period. Subsequent supervision, institutional learning and the management of new risks belong to continuing financial administration. The surviving official summary supports the dates, the mechanism and the reported total, but cannot substitute for detailed case records. The modern comparison with the Xiao Xiang concerns the difference between finishing one phase and eliminating all future uncertainty; it is not a claim about the motives of those who administered the fund.

01 乾 | Hexagram 01▶

01 乾 | Hexagram 01

B EUUS-WL-H01 · Rome, Europe · 458 BCE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Cincinnatus returns to his farm. Rome faced a military emergency and appointed Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus dictator, an extraordinary office with broad authority. Ancient tradition presents him as a landowner who had been away from ordinary public office when the summons came. He accepted the appointment, organized the Roman response, and after the emergency relinquished the dictatorship rather than keeping exceptional power. He then returned to private life and agricultural work. The episode was later retold as an example of temporary service rather than permanent possession of office. The historical details come through later Roman writers and should not be treated as a complete contemporary record. Even so, the sequence is clear in the tradition: urgent public duty interrupted private work, the task was completed, and the office was surrendered. His return to the farm became part of his long afterlife in European and American civic culture. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

Interpretive analogy Read Hexagram 01 retrospectively as a workplace and life-decision lens, not as evidence that the historical participants consulted the Zhouyi. Creative capacity matters, but finishing a demanding assignment can include knowing when to release authority and return to ordinary life. The case of Cincinnatus returns to his farm makes the comparison concrete because the decision changed how work, responsibility, or personal direction was organized. The useful takeaway is not to copy the historical choice mechanically. It is to notice the structure of the decision: what had changed, what was still under the person’s control, what had to be given up, and what new obligation followed. For a modern reader, the practical question is: what part of your current situation deserves a deliberate choice instead of automatic continuation? A promotion, partnership, resignation, return, side project, caregiving duty, or change of field can look very different from the outside than it feels in daily life. Use the analogy to clarify tradeoffs, timing, and responsibility. This is an editorial comparison written today; the historical source supports the event only, not any documented use of the Zhouyi.

Historical event Gutenberg builds a printing enterprise. Johannes Gutenberg worked in a world where books were copied by hand or produced with labor-intensive methods. His printing project required more than one invention: movable metal type, ink, presses, skilled labor, paper, and substantial financing had to work together. In Mainz he entered financial arrangements with Johann Fust and developed a workshop capable of producing large printed works, including the Bible associated with his name. The enterprise required repeated experiments and expensive equipment before revenue could be realized. A later legal dispute with Fust affected control of the workshop and its assets. Printing nevertheless spread rapidly through European cities after the 1450s. Gutenberg did not personally control the entire industry that followed, but the system demonstrated that standardized text production could be organized as a repeatable business process. The case is a reminder that waiting during development can be active work when the product requires integration before launch. Historical event Benjamin Franklin establishes himself as a printer. Benjamin Franklin left his apprenticeship in Boston as a young man and arrived in Philadelphia with limited resources. Historical event Henry Ford introduces the five-dollar day. Ford Motor Company had introduced moving assembly-line methods that sharply increased automobile production, but repetitive factory work was associated with high employee turnover. Constant hiring and training threatened the efficiency gains of the production system. In 1914 Ford announced a five-dollar daily wage for qualifying workers, far above common factory pay at the time, along with a shorter eight-hour shift. The policy attracted large numbers of applicants and helped stabilize the workforce, though eligibility initially came with intrusive company oversight of workers’ private lives. The wage policy became one of the most famous workplace decisions of the industrial era and was linked to Ford’s ability to operate intensive mass production. It also shows the limits of a simple “high pay” story: compensation, control, productivity, and employee autonomy were intertwined. Great organizational power created the ability to reshape work, but also the responsibility to decide how far employer authority should extend. Historical event Oskar Schindler redirects his factory to protect workers. Oskar Schindler was a German businessman who acquired an enamelware factory in occupied Kraków during the Second World War and initially benefited from the wartime economy and the exploitation surrounding forced labor. As Nazi persecution intensified, he used his factory, contacts, bribes, and claims about essential war production to protect Jewish workers from deportation. In 1944 he moved many workers to a new factory at Brünnlitz in the Sudetenland, where they survived until the end of the war. The records include the well-known lists connected with those transfers. More than a thousand Jews associated with his factories survived. Schindler’s postwar business ventures were not notably successful, and he was later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations. The case involves an ethically complex transformation in the use of a workplace: an enterprise that began within an exploitative system became a means of sheltering people from it. Historical event Tim Berners-Lee helps keep the World Wide Web open. Tim Berners-Lee worked at CERN, where researchers needed better ways to share information across different computers and institutions. In 1989 he proposed a hypertext system that became the foundation of the World Wide Web. He developed core technologies including HTML, HTTP, and the first web server and browser. CERN later released the web software into the public domain, allowing others to build compatible sites and tools without paying licensing fees. Berners-Lee then moved to MIT and founded the World Wide Web Consortium to coordinate open standards. The web expanded far beyond the environment in which it was created and became basic infrastructure for communication, commerce, publishing, and software. The decision to support open standards did not settle every later problem of privacy, competition, or platform power. It left the system deliberately unfinished so that others could extend it. 007爻 Historical event Augustine leaves a rhetoric career. Augustine had built a career as a teacher of rhetoric and eventually held a prestigious teaching post in Milan. His work depended on education, public speaking, and the patronage networks of the late Roman world. During the 380s he withdrew from that professional path, was baptized in Milan in 387, and returned to North Africa. He formed a religious community, was ordained a priest at Hippo, and later became bishop. The transition replaced a career centered on rhetoric with one centered on pastoral, intellectual, and institutional work. He continued writing and teaching for decades, but within a different vocation and set of responsibilities. His later books drew on skills developed in his earlier education while serving a new audience and purpose. The decision did not erase the first career; it redirected capabilities acquired there into a different form of work and life. He formed a religious community, was ordained a priest at Hippo, and later became bishop. The transition replaced a career centered on rhetoric with one centered on pastoral, intellectual, and institutional work. He continued writing and teaching for decades, but within a different vocation and set of responsibilities. His later books drew on skills developed in his earlier education while serving a new audience and purpose. The decision did not erase the first career; it redirected capabilities acquired there into a different form of work and life. 013爻 Historical event Benedict establishes Monte Cassino. Benedict of Nursia lived during a period of political fragmentation in Italy. Religious communities already existed, but rules, leadership practices, and daily routines varied widely. He established a monastery at Monte Cassino and is associated with the Rule of Saint Benedict, which organized prayer, reading, manual labor, obedience, hospitality, and community life. The rule treated daily work as part of a disciplined common rhythm rather than as an activity separate from spiritual life. Benedictine communities later spread across Europe and adapted the rule to different places and centuries. The monastery became not simply a retreat but a durable institution with roles, schedules, shared resources, and procedures for leadership. The case shows how an uncertain beginning can become workable when ordinary routines are specified and repeated. 019爻 Historical event Hildegard founds Rupertsberg. Hildegard of Bingen became a leader within a religious community at Disibodenberg, where women lived under arrangements connected to a male monastery. As her community and reputation grew, the existing setting no longer matched all of its needs. She pursued the creation of a separate convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen. The move required ecclesiastical approval, property, construction, funding, and the transfer of a community. From the new base she managed correspondence, music, writing, religious duties, and relationships with patrons and church authorities. Rupertsberg became the center of her later work, and she eventually founded another house at Eibingen. The change illustrates a practical workplace decision inside a medieval institution: seeking a structure with greater operational independence while retaining obligations to a wider network. The result was not immediate freedom from constraint, but a new platform for sustained work. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. 025爻 Historical event Gutenberg builds a printing enterprise. Johannes Gutenberg worked in a world where books were copied by hand or produced with labor-intensive methods. His printing project required more than one invention: movable metal type, ink, presses, skilled labor, paper, and substantial financing had to work together. In Mainz he entered financial arrangements with Johann Fust and developed a workshop capable of producing large printed works, including the Bible associated with his name. The enterprise required repeated experiments and expensive equipment before revenue could be realized. A later legal dispute with Fust affected control of the workshop and its assets. Printing nevertheless spread rapidly through European cities after the 1450s. Gutenberg did not personally control the entire industry that followed, but the system demonstrated that standardized text production could be organized as a repeatable business process. The case is a reminder that waiting during development can be active work when the product requires integration before launch. 030爻 Historical event Gutenberg builds a printing enterprise. Johannes Gutenberg worked in a world where books were copied by hand or produced with labor-intensive methods. His printing project required more than one invention: movable metal type, ink, presses, skilled labor, paper, and substantial financing had to work together. In Mainz he entered financial arrangements with Johann Fust and developed a workshop capable of producing large printed works, including the Bible associated with his name. The enterprise required repeated experiments and expensive equipment before revenue could be realized. A later legal dispute with Fust affected control of the workshop and its assets. Printing nevertheless spread rapidly through European cities after the 1450s. Gutenberg did not personally control the entire industry that followed, but the system demonstrated that standardized text production could be organized as a repeatable business process. 031爻 Historical event Michelangelo accepts the Sistine ceiling commission. Michelangelo was known primarily as a sculptor when Pope Julius II commissioned him to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. The assignment was large, technically difficult, and outside the medium for which he had built his strongest reputation. He accepted the work and organized scaffolding, assistants, materials, and fresco production over several years. He revised the working process as the project developed and completed a vast sequence of figures across the ceiling. The commission interrupted other work and placed him inside a demanding patron relationship. The finished ceiling became one of the best-known works of Renaissance art and altered Michelangelo’s professional identity, making painting a central part of how later audiences understood him. The episode was not free of disagreement or pressure, but it shows a career decision in which conflict with role expectations did not prevent a person from completing work beyond the boundaries of an earlier specialty. Line 1 | TW-WL-H07-L1 | XIANG-U-07-02

037爻 Historical event Leonardo moves to Milan. Leonardo da Vinci trained and worked in Florence, but opportunities there were shared among many established artists and workshops. In the early 1480s he moved to Milan and entered the service of Ludovico Sforza. His work in Milan extended beyond painting. He designed court entertainments, studied engineering and anatomy, proposed military devices, and worked on projects including The Last Supper and a large equestrian monument that was never completed. Service at court required him to combine artistic ability with technical, organizational, and representational tasks. The Milan period lasted many years and broadened the range of Leonardo’s professional practice. Political change later forced him to leave, showing that a career built around a patron could also be vulnerable to the patron’s circumstances. The move nevertheless demonstrates how a deliberate change of environment can expand the range of work available to a skilled person. 043爻 Historical event Boulton and Watt form a partnership. James Watt had developed improvements to the steam engine but faced the usual difficulties of turning an invention into a reliable commercial product. Building engines required capital, manufacturing capability, customers, installation, and maintenance. Matthew Boulton brought an established manufacturing base at Soho and experience in business organization. Their partnership combined Watt’s engineering work with Boulton’s production resources and commercial network. They licensed and supplied engines for mines and factories while continuing to improve designs and manage technical problems in the field. The partnership became one of the best-known industrial collaborations of the eighteenth century. Its success depended less on a single inspired moment than on complementary roles maintained over time. The case illustrates workplace alliance: a specialist and an operator creating more value together because each supplied capabilities the other lacked. 049爻 Historical event Benjamin Franklin establishes himself as a printer. Benjamin Franklin left his apprenticeship in Boston as a young man and arrived in Philadelphia with limited resources. Printing was a skilled trade that required equipment, customers, credit, and reputation, none of which could be created instantly. He worked for other printers, traveled to London, returned to Philadelphia, and eventually entered business on his own. He built a printing shop, published the Pennsylvania Gazette, produced Poor Richard’s Almanack, and developed relationships through civic and commercial activity. The growth was incremental and depended on repeated small decisions about work, saving, partnerships, and public reliability. The printing business gave Franklin financial independence and a platform for later scientific and civic work. His path was not a straight promotion inside one employer; it was a sequence of apprenticeships, moves, experiments, and accumulated credibility. The case shows how modest gains can compound before a career appears established from the outside. 055爻 Historical event Charles Darwin accepts the Beagle voyage. After university, Charles Darwin had not settled into a conventional profession. An opportunity arose to join HMS Beagle as a gentleman companion and naturalist on a surveying voyage, but the journey promised years away from home and no guaranteed career outcome. Darwin accepted after family discussion and sailed in 1831. During the voyage he collected specimens, recorded geological observations, corresponded with scientists, and encountered environments across South America and the Pacific. The work required careful routines of note-taking, preservation, comparison, and shipment back to Britain. When he returned in 1836, the collections and observations helped establish his scientific reputation. Years of further research followed before he published On the Origin of Species in 1859. The initial decision did not produce an immediate breakthrough; it placed him on a path where disciplined observation created options that had not existed before the voyage. 061爻 Historical event Bell Labs organizes the transistor team. Telephone networks needed more reliable and efficient electronic components than vacuum tubes could provide for many applications. Bell Labs had the resources to pursue fundamental physics and practical engineering in the same organization. A team including John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley worked on semiconductor problems. In 1947 Bardeen and Brattain demonstrated a working point-contact transistor, while Shockley later developed the junction transistor concept. The work involved theory, experiments, measurement, fabrication, and institutional support rather than a solitary invention. The transistor became a foundational technology for modern electronics. The individual relationships within the team later became strained, but the initial research environment demonstrated the value of assembling complementary expertise around a shared technical problem. Progress came from interaction among roles that could not be collapsed into one job description. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. Line 1 | TW-WL-H12-L1 | XIANG-U-12-02

067爻 Historical event Kodak develops but delays digital photography. Eastman Kodak dominated film photography when engineer Steven Sasson was asked to explore a new solid-state imaging technology. In 1975 he built an early self-contained digital camera prototype using a CCD sensor and digital storage. The prototype showed that photographs could be captured without film, but the image quality, speed, storage, and display ecosystem were still primitive. Kodak continued research and obtained important digital-imaging patents while its existing business remained tied to film, processing, and photographic paper. Over subsequent decades competitors and new consumer electronics companies advanced digital cameras and later camera phones. Kodak eventually sold digital products, but the transition undermined the economics of its historical core business. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 2012 and later emerged as a smaller business. The case is useful as a workplace decision story because recognizing a new technology and reorganizing around it are different tasks. 072爻 Historical event Kodak develops but delays digital photography. Eastman Kodak dominated film photography when engineer Steven Sasson was asked to explore a new solid-state imaging technology. The prototype showed that photographs could be captured without film, but the image quality, speed, storage, and display ecosystem were still primitive. Kodak continued research and obtained important digital-imaging patents while its existing business remained tied to film, processing, and photographic paper. Over subsequent decades competitors and new consumer electronics companies advanced digital cameras and later camera phones. Kodak eventually sold digital products, but the transition undermined the economics of its historical core business. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 2012 and later emerged as a smaller business. 073爻 Historical event Hewlett and Packard build a company partnership. Bill Hewlett and David Packard met as engineering students at Stanford and later explored the idea of building electronic instruments. They started a small business in a rented garage in Palo Alto in 1939. Their early work included an audio oscillator that found a customer in Walt Disney Studios. As the company grew, the founders developed management practices that emphasized technical competence, decentralized responsibility, and respect for employees. HP expanded from instruments into computing and other technologies over several decades. The company’s later history included major restructurings and splits, but its early partnership became an influential example of Silicon Valley company building. 079爻 Historical event Andrew Carnegie sells Carnegie Steel. Andrew Carnegie had built one of the largest steel businesses in the United States through investment in plants, technology, transportation, and aggressive cost control. By the end of the nineteenth century he was extremely wealthy and still associated with a demanding industrial enterprise. In 1901 J. P. Morgan organized the purchase of Carnegie Steel and combined it with other businesses to form U.S. Steel. Carnegie left active steel management with a fortune that made him one of the richest individuals of his era. He then devoted much of his remaining life to philanthropy, funding libraries, education, research, and foundations. The sale changed both his professional identity and the use of his resources. It did not erase controversies surrounding labor relations in the steel industry, including the Homestead conflict. As a life decision, the case shows that possessing more resources creates a second question: whether to keep maximizing the activity that created them or redirect them toward a different purpose. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. 085爻 Historical event George Washington Carver joins Tuskegee. George Washington Carver trained in agriculture and earned a graduate degree at Iowa State Agricultural College. In 1896 Booker T. Washington invited him to lead agricultural work at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. Carver accepted and spent much of his career at Tuskegee, teaching, conducting experiments, and producing practical bulletins for farmers. His work emphasized crop rotation, soil improvement, and uses for crops such as peanuts and sweet potatoes. Facilities and resources were limited compared with major research institutions, so he often worked with modest equipment and materials. Carver became nationally known, although popular stories later exaggerated some claims about his inventions. His long tenure shows a career decision shaped by mission and service rather than by the most prestigious laboratory setting. He used scientific training in an institution where education, extension work, and community needs were closely connected. 091爻 Historical event Walt Disney commits to Snow White. By the mid-1930s Walt Disney’s studio was successful with animated shorts, but a feature-length animated film had not yet been proven as a commercial format in Hollywood. Producing one would require years of work, new artistic methods, training, and large financial commitments. Disney committed the studio to Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. Costs rose as the project expanded, and the company had to manage thousands of drawings, music, story development, effects, and production schedules. The film premiered in 1937 and was released widely in 1938. Its commercial success gave the studio resources and credibility for additional feature films and a larger production organization. The decision also increased the scale and complexity of the workplace. Enthusiasm created momentum, but the result depended on turning excitement into systems that could coordinate many specialized workers over a long project. 097爻 Historical event Intel exits the memory-chip business. Intel had been built around semiconductor memory, but by the early 1980s Japanese competitors were putting intense pressure on the memory market. At the same time, microprocessors were becoming a more important part of Intel’s business. Company leaders, including Andy Grove and Gordon Moore, confronted the question of whether to keep defending the original product category or redirect resources. Intel gradually withdrew from dynamic random-access memory and concentrated more heavily on microprocessors. The shift affected factories, product priorities, staffing, and the company’s identity. The microprocessor strategy later became central to Intel’s growth during the personal-computer era. The case is often discussed as a strategic pivot, but it was also a workplace decision involving what skills, investments, and habits the organization would continue to follow. Adaptation required letting go of a business that had once defined the company. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Line 1 | TW-WL-H19-L1 | XIANG-U-19-02

109爻 Historical event Howard Schultz returns to Starbucks. Starbucks expanded rapidly during the 1990s and 2000s, but by the financial crisis the company faced slowing sales, store closures, and criticism that rapid growth had weakened parts of the customer experience. Howard Schultz had stepped away from the chief executive role while remaining chairman. He returned as CEO in 2008. Starbucks closed underperforming stores, slowed expansion, retrained baristas, and refocused on coffee quality, store experience, and digital loyalty programs. One highly publicized decision temporarily closed many U.S. stores for employee training. The company recovered and resumed growth, though it continued to face labor, market, and competitive issues in later years. The case shows the decision to approach a struggling organization directly rather than manage it only through financial targets. Returning leadership mattered because it was paired with operational changes visible to employees and customers. 115爻 Historical event Peter Drucker chooses an independent knowledge-work career. Peter Drucker worked in banking, journalism, research, teaching, and consulting across Europe and the United States. Rather than building a conventional executive career inside one corporation, he developed a professional life around studying how organizations worked. 121爻 Historical event Frances Perkins accepts the labor secretary role. Frances Perkins had spent years working on labor, workplace safety, and social reform in New York. The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire of 1911 became part of the context in which reformers pushed for stronger workplace protections. In 1933 President Franklin D. Roosevelt appointed Perkins Secretary of Labor, making her the first woman to serve in a U.S. presidential cabinet. She entered national office during the Great Depression and worked on employment policy, labor standards, and the development of Social Security legislation. Perkins served for twelve years and helped shape institutions that outlasted the immediate crisis. The role required moving from advocacy and state-level administration into a federal workplace where negotiation, legislation, bureaucracy, and political opposition were unavoidable. The career decision expanded her influence but also increased the scale of accountability. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 127爻 Historical event Coco Chanel reopens her fashion house. Coco Chanel had closed her couture house during the Second World War and spent years outside the active Paris fashion business. By the early 1950s the industry had changed, and Christian Dior’s highly structured postwar styles dominated attention. In 1954, in her seventies, Chanel reopened her couture house and presented new collections based on the simpler lines, jersey, suits, and practical movement long associated with her work. French reviews were initially mixed, while American buyers and press were more receptive. The business gradually regained influence. Chanel’s return extended her career and helped establish styles that remained central to the brand after her death. The case is a workplace decision about re-entry: returning after a long absence without simply reproducing the old market. Presentation mattered, but the comeback depended on whether the product still solved practical needs for customers. 139爻 Historical event Steve Jobs returns to Apple. Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985 after conflicts over the company’s direction and spent the next decade building NeXT and helping develop Pixar. Apple later struggled with an overly broad product line, operating-system problems, and financial losses. Apple acquired NeXT in 1997, bringing Jobs back as an adviser and then interim chief executive. The company simplified its products, ended or reduced several projects, formed a new relationship with Microsoft, and concentrated on a smaller set of hardware and software priorities. The iMac followed in 1998, and later products expanded the company into music, phones, and tablets. Jobs’s return did not simply restore the Apple of the early 1980s. It used experience gained elsewhere to build a different organization around fewer priorities. The case is about return after separation: coming back can work when the person and the workplace have both changed enough to avoid replaying the old pattern. 151爻 Historical event Warren Buffett closes his investment partnership. Warren Buffett had managed investment partnerships through the 1950s and 1960s using a value-oriented approach. By the late 1960s he judged the market environment less attractive for the methods and opportunities he had relied upon. In 1969 he dissolved the partnerships rather than continue simply because the structure had been successful. Investors received cash and securities, including interests connected with Berkshire Hathaway. Buffett then concentrated more heavily on Berkshire as a vehicle for owning businesses and investments over long periods. Berkshire later became a large conglomerate and investment company. The decision to stop one successful arrangement before beginning another is useful in a workplace and life context because it shows accumulation paired with restraint.
