157爻 Historical event Alice Waters opens Chez Panisse. Alice Waters had studied in France and developed an interest in food shaped by fresh ingredients and shared meals. She did not begin with a conventional career path as a trained restaurant chef or hospitality executive. In 1971 she and collaborators opened Chez Panisse in Berkeley. The restaurant gradually built relationships with local farmers and suppliers and emphasized seasonal ingredients and simple preparation. Operations changed over time as the team learned how to run a restaurant, source consistent produce, and translate ideals about food into daily service. Chez Panisse became influential in American cooking and in discussions of local agriculture, school food, and sustainable sourcing. The work shows nourishment as an operational decision: values about health, quality, and community become meaningful only when purchasing, menus, schedules, and supplier relationships support them every day. Line 1 | TW-WL-H28-L1 | XIANG-U-28-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H28-L1 | XIANG-U-28-02

163爻 Historical event NASA flight controllers manage Apollo 13. Apollo 13 launched in April 1970 as a planned lunar-landing mission. An oxygen tank explosion crippled the spacecraft on the way to the Moon, damaging electrical and life-support systems and ending the landing objective. Astronauts and NASA teams in Mission Control shifted immediately from exploration to survival. They used the lunar module as a lifeboat, conserved power and water, revised navigation procedures, and developed a method for adapting carbon-dioxide filters with materials available onboard. Engineers tested procedures on the ground before sending instructions to the crew. The astronauts returned safely to Earth. The mission was later studied as an example of crisis management, technical teamwork, and decision-making under constrained resources. The case shows a structure under excessive load: success came not from insisting on the original goal, but from redefining the goal and reducing demands to what the damaged system could still support. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 169爻 Historical event Grace Hopper develops compiler ideas. Grace Hopper left an academic mathematics career to join the U.S. Naval Reserve during the Second World War and was assigned to work with the Harvard Mark I computer. Early programming required detailed manipulation of machine-oriented instructions. After the war she continued in computing and advocated systems that would let programmers work with more human-readable commands. At Remington Rand she helped develop compiler technology and contributed to efforts that led toward COBOL, a language designed for business data processing. Her work connected programming, documentation, standards, and communication across technical and business users. Compilers and higher-level languages became fundamental to software development. Hopper’s career also became an example of repeated transition: academia to military service, then industry, standards work, and later senior naval leadership. The case shows how clarity can be built by creating interfaces that let more people participate in complex work. 175爻 Historical event Julia Child retrains in French cooking. Julia Child moved to France after the Second World War because of her husband Paul Child’s diplomatic posting. She had worked in wartime government service but had not established a professional career in food. In Paris she studied at Le Cordon Bleu, practiced intensively, and later collaborated with Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle on a French cookbook for American readers. The manuscript went through years of testing, revision, and publishing difficulty before Mastering the Art of French Cooking appeared in 1961. Child then moved into television, where she demonstrated techniques for a mass audience. Her second career became highly influential in American food culture. The transition was gradual and collaborative rather than a single act of reinvention. It shows influence growing through shared work, repeated practice, and the ability to translate expertise from one culture and professional setting into another. Line 1 | TW-WL-H33-L1 | XIANG-L-33-02

193爻 Historical event Henry Ford introduces the five-dollar day. Ford Motor Company had introduced moving assembly-line methods that sharply increased automobile production, but repetitive factory work was associated with high employee turnover. Constant hiring and training threatened the efficiency gains of the production system. In 1914 Ford announced a five-dollar daily wage for qualifying workers, far above common factory pay at the time, along with a shorter eight-hour shift. The policy attracted large numbers of applicants and helped stabilize the workforce, though eligibility initially came with intrusive company oversight of workers’ private lives. The wage policy became one of the most famous workplace decisions of the industrial era and was linked to Ford’s ability to operate intensive mass production. It also shows the limits of a simple “high pay” story: compensation, control, productivity, and employee autonomy were intertwined. Great organizational power created the ability to reshape work, but also the responsibility to decide how far employer authority should extend. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Line 5 | TW-WL-H33-L5 | XIANG-L-33-06

197爻 Historical event Henry Ford introduces the five-dollar day. Ford Motor Company had introduced moving assembly-line methods that sharply increased automobile production, but repetitive factory work was associated with high employee turnover. Constant hiring and training threatened the efficiency gains of the production system. In 1914 Ford announced a five-dollar daily wage for qualifying workers, far above common factory pay at the time, along with a shorter eight-hour shift. The policy attracted large numbers of applicants and helped stabilize the workforce, though eligibility initially came with intrusive company oversight of workers’ private lives. The wage policy became one of the most famous workplace decisions of the industrial era and was linked to Ford’s ability to operate intensive mass production. It also shows the limits of a simple “high pay” story: compensation, control, productivity, and employee autonomy were intertwined. Great organizational power created the ability to reshape work, but also the responsibility to decide how far employer authority should extend. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

199爻 Historical event Katherine Johnson accepts aerospace research work. Katherine Johnson had trained as a mathematician and worked as a teacher before learning that the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics was hiring women mathematicians. Segregation and gender barriers sharply constrained professional opportunities for Black women in technical fields. She joined the West Area Computing unit at Langley in 1953 and later moved into flight research. Johnson calculated and checked trajectories for early U.S. space missions, including work connected with John Glenn’s orbital flight and later Apollo missions. Her role grew as she asked to attend technical briefings and contribute directly to analytical work that had often been separated by job classification. Johnson spent decades at NASA and became widely recognized much later in life for work that had previously been less visible to the public. The career demonstrates progress through both skill and institutional access: advancement can require not only doing excellent work, but also gaining entry to the rooms where decisions are made. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Historical case EUUS-WL-H35: Oskar Schindler redirects his factory to protect workers · Occupied Poland and Czechoslovakia, Europe · 1939–1945

Line 1 | TW-WL-H35-L1 | XIANG-L-35-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H35-L1 | XIANG-L-35-02

205爻 Historical event Oskar Schindler redirects his factory to protect workers. Oskar Schindler was a German businessman who acquired an enamelware factory in occupied Kraków during the Second World War and initially benefited from the wartime economy and the exploitation surrounding forced labor. As Nazi persecution intensified, he used his factory, contacts, bribes, and claims about essential war production to protect Jewish workers from deportation. In 1944 he moved many workers to a new factory at Brünnlitz in the Sudetenland, where they survived until the end of the war. The records include the well-known lists connected with those transfers. More than a thousand Jews associated with his factories survived. Schindler’s postwar business ventures were not notably successful, and he was later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations. The case involves an ethically complex transformation in the use of a workplace: an enterprise that began within an exploitative system became a means of sheltering people from it. 211爻 Historical event Eleanor Roosevelt builds an independent public role. Eleanor Roosevelt’s public life developed within a prominent political family, but she gradually built activities that were not reducible to her husband Franklin Roosevelt’s career. She taught, worked with reform organizations, wrote, and developed political networks before becoming first lady. In the White House she traveled extensively, held women-only press conferences, wrote a syndicated column, and reported on social and labor conditions. After Franklin Roosevelt’s death she continued public work, serving as a U.S. delegate to the United Nations and chairing the committee involved in drafting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Her long career shows a household and professional decision intertwined: family position created obligations and access, but she developed a separate working identity through repeated public responsibilities. The shift did not occur in one dramatic break; it emerged through accumulated roles that eventually became independent of the original family office. Line 1 | TW-WL-H38-L1 | XIANG-L-38-02

223爻 Historical event Ludwig van Beethoven continues composing after severe hearing loss. Beethoven built his career as a pianist and composer in Vienna, but his hearing deteriorated while he was still relatively young. For a professional musician, the loss threatened both public performance and ordinary communication. He reduced his performing career but continued composing, increasingly relying on written conversation and his internal knowledge of musical structure. Major works from his later years included symphonies, piano sonatas, string quartets, and the Missa solemnis. His working methods adapted around the disability rather than restoring the earlier conditions of his career. Beethoven died in 1827 with a body of late work that became central to the classical repertoire. The story is not one of “overcoming” a disability as if the loss were unimportant. It is a practical example of redesigning work when a core ability changes: reducing some activities, relying more heavily on others, and preserving the part of the vocation that remained possible. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 229爻 Historical event Patagonia transfers ownership to mission-focused entities. Patagonia grew from a climbing-equipment business associated with Yvon Chouinard into a global outdoor-apparel company with a long record of environmental advocacy. By the 2010s the question of succession and ownership had become important because the company’s value and influence extended beyond its founder. In 2022 the Chouinard family transferred voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust and nonvoting stock to the Holdfast Collective, a nonprofit organized to use distributions for environmental purposes. The company continued operating as a for-profit business, but the ownership structure was redesigned so that control and economic benefits were directed toward stated long-term goals. The arrangement attracted praise and scrutiny over governance, taxes, and accountability. Whatever view one takes of the structure, it represents a deliberate decrease in conventional family ownership rights in exchange for a mission-oriented succession plan. The life decision concerned what to give up in order to preserve a chosen purpose after the founder’s active role. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward.

235爻 Historical event Sara Blakely starts Spanx while keeping her day job. Sara Blakely was selling fax machines door to door when she began developing an idea for footless shaping hosiery. She had limited experience in apparel manufacturing and did not initially leave her paid job to pursue the idea full-time. She researched patents, contacted hosiery manufacturers, developed prototypes, and used personal savings rather than outside venture capital. After finding a manufacturer willing to produce the product, she worked on packaging and retail outreach. Spanx launched in 2000 and gained national distribution after early retail success and publicity. Blakely later became a prominent entrepreneur and sold a majority stake in Spanx to Blackstone in 2021 while remaining involved. The early sequence shows increase built through bounded risk: the project advanced before the founder abandoned all income and before the market had validated the concept. 241爻 Historical event Johnson & Johnson recalls Tylenol. In 1982 several people in the Chicago area died after taking Tylenol capsules that had been maliciously contaminated with cyanide after manufacture. The deaths created an immediate public-safety crisis for Johnson & Johnson and its McNeil Consumer Products subsidiary. The company warned consumers, cooperated with authorities, and removed Tylenol capsules from the market in a large nationwide recall. It later reintroduced the product with tamper-resistant packaging and other safety changes. The contamination was not caused by the normal manufacturing process, but the company still had to decide how much action to take before every fact was known. Tylenol eventually recovered much of its market position, and tamper-evident packaging became standard across the industry. The case is frequently used in management education because the decisive act was public and costly: the organization treated a product-safety boundary as more important than protecting short-term sales. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Line 1 | TW-WL-H42-L1 | XIANG-L-42-02

247爻 Historical event Bill Gates and Paul Allen form Microsoft. Bill Gates and Paul Allen had worked together with computers as students and followed the emerging market for personal computers. In 1975 they saw information about the Altair 8800 and contacted its maker with a proposal to provide a BASIC interpreter. They developed the software and formed Microsoft, initially based in Albuquerque near the customer. The company later moved to the Seattle area and built a business licensing software to multiple hardware manufacturers. Their roles and ownership evolved as the company expanded and as Allen later stepped back because of illness. Microsoft became one of the world’s largest technology companies. The founding story is useful as an encounter case because an external development—the appearance of an affordable microcomputer kit—met existing skills and a long-running partnership. 253爻 Historical event Pixar organizes a collaborative story process. Pixar began as a computer-graphics technology company and gradually shifted toward making animated feature films. Producing a film required artists, writers, engineers, directors, editors, and executives to coordinate over several years. As the studio developed movies such as Toy Story, it built practices for repeated internal review, candid feedback, and revision. The group later known as the “Braintrust” became one visible expression of a broader culture in which work-in-progress could be criticized by peers without transferring formal control of the project away from its director. Pixar produced a long run of commercially successful films and became part of Disney in 2006. Like all creative organizations, it also faced management and cultural challenges. The relevant workplace decision is structural: gathering talented people is not enough; the organization must create a process through which they can improve one another’s work without turning feedback into ownership competition. 258爻 Historical event Pixar organizes a collaborative story process. Pixar began as a computer-graphics technology company and gradually shifted toward making animated feature films. Producing a film required artists, writers, engineers, directors, editors, and executives to coordinate over several years. As the studio developed movies such as Toy Story, it built practices for repeated internal review, candid feedback, and revision. The group later known as the “Braintrust” became one visible expression of a broader culture in which work-in-progress could be criticized by peers without transferring formal control of the project away from its director. Pixar produced a long run of commercially successful films and became part of Disney in 2006. Like all creative organizations, it also faced management and cultural challenges. The relevant workplace decision is structural: gathering talented people is not enough; the organization must create a process through which they can improve one another’s work without turning feedback into ownership competition. 259爻 Historical event Ursula Burns rises through Xerox and becomes CEO. Ursula Burns joined Xerox as a mechanical-engineering intern in 1980 while completing graduate study. She entered a large technology company at a time when leadership ranks in major U.S. corporations included very few Black women. Burns moved through engineering, product development, operations, and senior management roles. She worked with successive chief executives, took responsibility for major business units, and became president of Xerox before being named chief executive in 2009. Her promotion made her the first Black woman to lead a Fortune 500 company. As CEO she oversaw a major services acquisition and later changes in company structure before stepping down in 2016. Her career illustrates ascent as a sequence rather than a sudden appointment. Technical work, line responsibility, sponsorship, and exposure to different parts of the business accumulated until the organization could evaluate her for enterprise leadership. 265爻 Historical event Oprah Winfrey moves from Baltimore television to Chicago. Oprah Winfrey began working in radio and television news while still young and became an anchor in Baltimore. The fit with conventional evening-news presentation was poor, and she was moved from the anchor desk into a daytime talk format. That change led her toward a style of interviewing and audience interaction that suited her abilities more closely. In 1984 she moved to Chicago to host AM Chicago, which quickly improved its ratings. The program was expanded and renamed The Oprah Winfrey Show, becoming nationally syndicated in 1986. Winfrey later built a media company, production business, magazine, and television network. The career path shows constraint turning into redirection: a setback in one professional format became the occasion to identify a different format in which the same communication skills were more effective. The later success does not make the early dismissal pleasant, but it changed the meaning of the next decision. Line 1 | TW-WL-H46-L1 | XIANG-L-46-02

271爻 Historical event Mayo Clinic develops a group-practice model. William Worrall Mayo and his sons William and Charles developed a medical practice in Rochester, Minnesota, that grew after collaboration with other physicians and with the Sisters of Saint Francis following the 1883 tornado. As patient volume and medical complexity increased, the practice recruited specialists and organized care around shared records, laboratories, salaried physicians, and consultation across disciplines. The model differed from a solo-practice arrangement in which one physician tried to own every part of diagnosis and treatment. The Mayo Clinic became a major medical and research institution. Its history includes many later expansions, but the early organizational decision is clear: expertise was treated as a common resource that could be drawn upon by teams. The “well” in this workplace story is not one star physician; it is the institutional system that makes accumulated knowledge available to patients and colleagues. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. Historical case EUUS-WL-H47: Netflix shifts from DVDs to streaming · United States · 2007 onward

Line 1 | TW-WL-H47-L1 | XIANG-L-47-02▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H47-L1 | XIANG-L-47-02

277爻 Historical event Netflix shifts from DVDs to streaming. Netflix began as a DVD-by-mail rental service and built its early business around subscriptions, logistics, and a large physical catalog. Improvements in broadband created a path for video delivery that could eventually reduce the need to mail discs. In 2007 Netflix introduced streaming for subscribers and gradually invested more heavily in the new mode of delivery. The transition required licensing, software, devices, data infrastructure, and eventually original programming. In 2011 a poorly received attempt to separate the DVD business under the name Qwikster was quickly reversed after customer backlash. Streaming ultimately became the center of Netflix’s business while the DVD service was wound down years later. The case is a workplace transformation rather than a clean one-time pivot: the company had to change technology, contracts, skills, and customer habits while still operating the old model. Some experiments worked; others were reversed. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Historical case EUUS-WL-H48: Alfred Nobel creates the Nobel Prizes through his will · Europe · 1895–1901

Line 1 | TW-WL-H48-L1 | XIANG-L-48-02

283爻 Historical event Alfred Nobel creates the Nobel Prizes through his will. Alfred Nobel became wealthy through inventions, patents, and businesses connected with explosives and industrial technology. By the 1890s he had accumulated a large estate spread across several countries. In 1895 he signed a will directing most of his fortune into a fund whose investment income would support annual prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, and peace. The instructions surprised some relatives and required years of legal and organizational work after his death in 1896. The Nobel Foundation was established to administer the assets and prizes. The first prizes were awarded in 1901, creating an institution that continued far beyond Nobel’s own business career. The decision transformed private wealth into a recurring public process with rules, committees, investment management, and international recognition. The “cauldron” is institutional: resources are converted into a different form of value through a durable container. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 289爻 Historical event Johnson Space Center responds to the Challenger disaster. The Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart shortly after launch on January 28, 1986, killing all seven crew members. The disaster shocked NASA and halted the shuttle program while investigators examined technical and organizational causes. The Rogers Commission identified the failure of an O-ring seal in unusually cold conditions and criticized decision processes surrounding the launch. NASA redesigned solid rocket booster joints, changed management and safety practices, and did not resume shuttle flights until 1988. The return to flight came after testing, review, and organizational changes rather than a rapid attempt to restore the schedule. The Challenger case remains a central example in engineering ethics and organizational communication because warnings, hierarchy, schedule pressure, and technical uncertainty interacted. Shock was not itself a lesson; the lesson depended on whether the institution preserved evidence and changed the system that had produced the decision. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

Line 1 | TW-WL-H50-L1 | XIANG-L-50-02

295爻 Historical event Bill Watterson ends Calvin and Hobbes. Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes became one of the most widely read newspaper comic strips of its era. Its success created strong demand for licensing, merchandising, and continued publication. Watterson resisted most merchandising and fought for greater control over page layout and artistic presentation. In 1995 he announced that he would end the strip at the end of the year, despite its popularity and commercial value. The final installment appeared on December 31, 1995. Watterson largely withdrew from the public commercial comics industry afterward and pursued private artistic interests. The decision demonstrates keeping still as a career choice: stopping can be intentional when continuing would require compromises the creator does not want to make. It also shows that the market’s willingness to buy more does not create an obligation to produce more. Line 6 | TW-WL-H50-L6 | XIANG-L-50-07

300爻 Historical event Bill Watterson ends Calvin and Hobbes. Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes became one of the most widely read newspaper comic strips of its era. Its success created strong demand for licensing, merchandising, and continued publication. Watterson resisted most merchandising and fought for greater control over page layout and artistic presentation. In 1995 he announced that he would end the strip at the end of the year, despite its popularity and commercial value. The final installment appeared on December 31, 1995. Watterson largely withdrew from the public commercial comics industry afterward and pursued private artistic interests. The decision demonstrates keeping still as a career choice: stopping can be intentional when continuing would require compromises the creator does not want to make. It also shows that the market’s willingness to buy more does not create an obligation to produce more. 301爻 Historical event Vera Wang shifts from skating and publishing to fashion. Vera Wang trained seriously as a figure skater and competed at a high level, but she did not make the U.S. Olympic team. She then moved into fashion publishing and spent many years at Vogue before working at Ralph Lauren. When planning her own wedding, she became dissatisfied with available bridal options and eventually entered bridal design. In 1990 she opened a bridal boutique in New York, first carrying established designers and then developing her own collections. The business expanded into a global fashion brand. The path was gradual and built on skills from earlier stages: discipline from sport, visual judgment from editorial work, and industry knowledge from fashion companies. The case shows that a career change does not have to discard previous identities. Progress can be sequential, with each stage supplying capabilities that make the next stage more credible. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. 307爻 Historical event Martha Stewart turns a catering business into a media career. Martha Stewart worked in modeling and then as a stockbroker before moving with her family to Connecticut. She developed skills in cooking, entertaining, gardening, and home renovation while building a local catering business. The catering work led to publishing opportunities. Her first book, Entertaining, appeared in 1982, followed by additional books, television appearances, a magazine, and eventually Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia. The business connected practical domestic activities with publishing, retail, licensing, and broadcast media. Her later career included serious legal and corporate setbacks, followed by continued business activity after imprisonment. The earlier transition is useful as a life-and-work case because it turned activities often treated as private household labor into a structured professional platform. 309爻 Historical event Martha Stewart turns a catering business into a media career. Martha Stewart worked in modeling and then as a stockbroker before moving with her family to Connecticut. She developed skills in cooking, entertaining, gardening, and home renovation while building a local catering business. The catering work led to publishing opportunities. Her first book, Entertaining, appeared in 1982, followed by additional books, television appearances, a magazine, and eventually Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia. The business connected practical domestic activities with publishing, retail, licensing, and broadcast media. Her later career included serious legal and corporate setbacks, followed by continued business activity after imprisonment. The earlier transition is useful as a life-and-work case because it turned activities often treated as private household labor into a structured professional platform. The new career emerged from a different status relationship than her earlier finance job and required redefining what counted as marketable expertise. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

313爻 Historical event Dolly Parton launches the Imagination Library. Dolly Parton had built a successful music and entertainment career before creating the Imagination Library in 1995 through the Dollywood Foundation. The program began in her home county in Tennessee and was inspired in part by her father’s limited formal education. The program mails age-appropriate books to enrolled children from birth until school age. It expanded through partnerships with local communities that share the work and funding needed to operate the program in different regions. Over time it spread across the United States and into other countries. The project became a large literacy initiative independent of any single album or performance cycle. It demonstrates abundance redirected toward a recurring public benefit: celebrity, organizational capacity, and financial resources were used to build an institution that functions through distributed local participation. 319爻 Historical event Mark Twain leaves riverboating and builds a writing career. Samuel Clemens trained and worked as a Mississippi River pilot before the American Civil War disrupted commercial river traffic. The occupation had required technical knowledge, navigation, and a specific regional economy. He traveled west, tried mining, worked in journalism, and began publishing humorous sketches under the name Mark Twain. Reporting assignments and travel supplied material for books, and his lecture career added another source of income and public visibility. Writing gradually replaced his earlier occupational identity. Twain became one of the best-known American authors, but he also experienced business failures and financial problems later in life. The traveler theme is practical: moving through places and jobs did not guarantee success, yet each environment supplied observations, contacts, and material that made a different career possible. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. Line 1 | TW-WL-H55-L1 | XIANG-L-55-02 | Record 325▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H55-L1 | XIANG-L-55-02 | Record 325

325爻 Historical event IKEA standardizes flat-pack furniture. Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA in Sweden as a mail-order business and gradually focused it on furniture. Shipping assembled furniture was expensive and vulnerable to damage, limiting how efficiently products could reach customers. During the 1950s IKEA increasingly adopted flat-pack designs that customers could transport and assemble themselves. Designers worked within constraints of packaging, manufacturing, cost, and simple assembly. The company paired this with catalogs, large self-service stores, standardized product names, and a retail experience that explained the system to customers. The model expanded internationally and became closely associated with IKEA’s identity. Its influence was not based on one dramatic invention but on persistent design decisions that penetrated many parts of the business. Small operational choices reinforced one another until the whole customer experience worked differently. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The company paired this with catalogs, large self-service stores, standardized product names, and a retail experience that explained the system to customers. The model expanded internationally and became closely associated with IKEA’s identity. Its influence was not based on one dramatic invention but on persistent design decisions that penetrated many parts of the business. Small operational choices reinforced one another until the whole customer experience worked differently. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. LEGO entered the early 2000s with declining financial performance after expanding into many products and ventures beyond its traditional construction toys. 337爻 Historical event Automattic builds a distributed company. Automattic was founded around WordPress-related products and from an early stage hired people who worked from many locations rather than from a single headquarters. Distributed work was unusual for a growing technology company in the mid-2000s. The company developed written communication practices, online collaboration tools, periodic in-person gatherings, and hiring processes designed for remote work. Employees could live in different countries and time zones, which broadened recruiting but also increased the need for documentation and asynchronous coordination. Automattic grew into a large distributed organization and became a frequently cited example of remote-first work. The model is not free of tradeoffs; it requires deliberate communication and can make informal coordination harder. The case illustrates dispersion managed through common systems rather than through physical proximity. Line 1 | TW-WL-H58-L1 | XIANG-L-58-02 | Record 343▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H58-L1 | XIANG-L-58-02 | Record 343

343爻 Historical event Basecamp formalizes a forty-hour workweek culture. The software company 37signals, later known as Basecamp, built products with a relatively small team and publicly argued against the idea that long hours were a necessary sign of commitment in technology work. Its leaders wrote about limiting meetings, reducing simultaneous projects, using fixed cycles, and maintaining roughly forty-hour workweeks, with shorter weeks in some summer periods. These practices were tied to product choices that favored smaller teams and limited scope rather than constant expansion. The company remained private and profitable for many years, though its culture and policies also became controversial during later internal disputes. The workplace decision is about limitation: a boundary around hours and project load can support focus, but only if the organization also limits what it promises customers and itself. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. Line 1 | TW-WL-H59-L1 | XIANG-L-59-02 | Record 349▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H59-L1 | XIANG-L-59-02 | Record 349

349爻 Historical event Cadbury develops Bournville as a worker community. Cadbury expanded chocolate manufacturing near Birmingham during the nineteenth century. As the business grew, George and Richard Cadbury moved production to a less crowded site at Bournville, where there was room for a larger factory and a different environment around it. The company and related trusts developed housing, green space, recreation, and community facilities for workers and residents. The model reflected Quaker social ideas as well as practical concerns about health, stability, and the conditions of industrial employment. It was still a company-centered environment, and later observers have debated the balance between welfare and paternalism. Bournville influenced discussions of model villages and employer responsibility. The case is useful for inner truth because stated values were made visible in physical investment. Credibility depended on whether workers could experience the policy in housing, sanitation, recreation, and workplace conditions rather than only in company language. Historical case EUUS-WL-H60: Southwest Airlines grows through a focused route model · United States · 1971 onward

Line 1 | TW-WL-H60-L1 | XIANG-L-60-02 | Record 355▶

Line 1 | TW-WL-H60-L1 | XIANG-L-60-02 | Record 355

355爻 Historical event Southwest Airlines grows through a focused route model. Southwest Airlines began service in Texas in 1971 after years of legal challenges from competing airlines. It entered a regulated industry with fewer resources than major carriers and initially focused on a small network of short routes. The airline emphasized quick aircraft turnaround, standardized fleets, point-to-point service, and simple fares. Growth came by adding routes and cities while trying to preserve operating routines that supported low costs. Expansion accelerated after U.S. airline deregulation, but the company generally avoided becoming a traditional hub-and-spoke network. Southwest became a major U.S. airline and was profitable for many years, though later operational disruptions and industry changes exposed weaknesses that required further investment. The historical growth pattern shows “small exceeding” as bounded expansion: doing many small operational things consistently before attempting every possible market. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. Line 1 | TW-WL-H61-L1 | XIANG-L-61-02 | Record 361

361爻 Historical event Apollo 11 team returns from the Moon and shifts to follow-on work. Apollo 11 achieved the first crewed lunar landing in July 1969 after years of engineering, testing, accidents, budget commitments, and work by a very large NASA and contractor workforce. The landing fulfilled the central public objective set for the Apollo program earlier in the decade. After the mission, Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins, flight controllers, engineers, and managers moved into different assignments. NASA still had additional Apollo missions, scientific goals, hardware decisions, and institutional questions to manage. The achievement did not eliminate risk, as later missions such as Apollo 13 demonstrated. Apollo 11 became a symbol of completion, but the program’s work continued and eventually ended after Apollo 17 in 1972. The case illustrates a common workplace problem after success: a milestone can create the illusion that the system no longer needs vigilance. Completion changes the task; it does not abolish the need for maintenance, learning, and decisions about what comes next. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. 367爻 Historical event Jeff Bezos leaves finance to start Amazon. Jeff Bezos worked in finance and technology roles in New York, including at the hedge fund D. E. Shaw. In the early 1990s he observed rapid growth in internet usage and considered business models that could take advantage of online distribution. In 1994 he left his job and moved to the Seattle area, where he founded Amazon as an online bookseller. The company began with a narrow category that benefited from a vast catalog and mail delivery, then expanded into other products, marketplaces, cloud computing, devices, and logistics. Growth required repeated reinvestment and tolerance for years in which profits were limited relative to expansion. Amazon became one of the largest companies in the world, while its labor practices, market power, and competitive effects remain subjects of debate. The initial life decision illustrates “before completion”: evidence can be strong enough to justify beginning even when the final business model is unknown. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. The situation created a constraint or opening; a person or team made a choice within the resources and institutions available; the result then created new responsibilities rather than a final ending. The record does not require invented dialogue or private motives to make the decision understandable. It can be followed through observable actions, roles, projects, and later consequences. The case also shows why career and life decisions are rarely isolated from context. Skills, money, family obligations, colleagues, technology, rules, and timing shape what options are realistically available. The decision can therefore be described without claiming that success was inevitable. What matters historically is the chain from the conditions before the choice, through the work required to carry it out, to the consequences that became visible afterward. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning. The value of the episode lies in the documented sequence of action and consequence, not in turning the person into a flawless model.

Line 1 | TW-WL-H64-L1 | XIANG-L-64-02 | Record 379

379爻 Historical event Tim Berners-Lee helps keep the World Wide Web open. Tim Berners-Lee worked at CERN, where researchers needed better ways to share information across different computers and institutions. In 1989 he proposed a hypertext system that became the foundation of the World Wide Web. He developed core technologies including HTML, HTTP, and the first web server and browser. CERN later released the web software into the public domain, allowing others to build compatible sites and tools without paying licensing fees. Berners-Lee then moved to MIT and founded the World Wide Web Consortium to coordinate open standards. The web expanded far beyond the environment in which it was created and became basic infrastructure for communication, commerce, publishing, and software. The decision to support open standards did not settle every later problem of privacy, competition, or platform power. It left the system deliberately unfinished so that others could extend it. Seen as a workplace and life-decision story, the important sequence is practical rather than dramatic. 383爻 Historical event Tim Berners-Lee helps keep the World Wide Web open. Tim Berners-Lee worked at CERN, where researchers needed better ways to share information across different computers and institutions. In 1989 he proposed a hypertext system that became the foundation of the World Wide Web. He developed core technologies including HTML, HTTP, and the first web server and browser. CERN later released the web software into the public domain, allowing others to build compatible sites and tools without paying licensing fees. Berners-Lee then moved to MIT and founded the World Wide Web Consortium to coordinate open standards. The web expanded far beyond the environment in which it was created and became basic infrastructure for communication, commerce, publishing, and software. The decision to support open standards did not settle every later problem of privacy, competition, or platform power. It left the system deliberately unfinished so that others could extend it. Later reputation can make the result look obvious, but it was not obvious at the beginning.
